Swerved
SWERVD
v. (turned aside; missed the mark; deviated)
Greek astocheo, from a-, not, and stochos, a mark or aim — to miss the target, to fail of the aim. The English swerve is Old English sweorfan, to rub or turn aside.

Biblical Definition

From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling. Paul is describing men who wanted to be teachers of the law and had missed something first. The Greek astocheo is an archer's word — to miss the mark, to fail of the aim — and the question is what mark they missed. Paul has just named it: now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned. The end is the target, the thing the commandment aims at, and it is love proceeding from three things — a clean heart, a conscience that works, and faith without pretence. Men who miss that target do not thereby stop teaching. They turn aside unto vain jangling — empty talk, disputation for its own sake — and Paul adds a devastating observation: desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm. The confidence survives the comprehension. This is the permanent hazard of doctrinal seriousness, and the dictionary names it against itself as readily as against anyone: a man may hold sound positions, defend them vigorously, and have swerved from the mark those positions exist to serve. Paul does not answer error with less doctrine but with doctrine aimed where it belongs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to wander from any line prescribed, or from a rule of duty; to deviate; to depart.

SWERVE, v.i. To wander; to rove; to stray; to deviate.

SWERVE, v.i. To wander from any line prescribed, or from a rule of duty; to depart; to deviate.

SWERVED, pp. Deviated; departed from the line or rule.

JANGLE, v.i. To quarrel in words; to altercate; to bicker; to wrangle.

AIM, n. The pointing or direction of a missile weapon; the direction of any thing to a particular point or object; intention; purpose.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 1:6 — "From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling;"

1 Timothy 1:5 — "Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned:"

1 Timothy 1:7 — "Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm."

2 Timothy 2:22 — "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart."

Modern Corruption

Doctrine and love are regularly set against each other, one party abandoning precision for warmth and the other treating contention as a proof of soundness; Paul makes love the mark that doctrine aims at.

expand to see more

One party reads 1 Timothy 1:5 as a demotion of doctrine: since the end of the commandment is charity, precision must matter less than kindness, and controversy is itself the failure. That inverts Paul's argument. He is writing to charge Timothy that certain men teach no other doctrine, and the whole letter is an exercise in doctrinal precision. An archer who cares nothing for his aim does not hit the target by good will. Love is the mark, and sound doctrine is how the shot is aimed; a church that abandons the aim in the name of the target will hit neither.

The opposite party swerves in the direction this verse actually describes, and it is the temptation of the confessionally serious. A man may be exactly right about the ordo salutis and have a conscience he no longer consults and a faith that has become a position he defends. Paul's diagnosis of the swerved is not that they became liberal but that they turned to vain jangling — endless, heated, empty dispute — while still desiring the teacher's chair. The test he supplies is not softness but the three things named in verse 5: a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. Doctrine that produces none of these has missed what it was aimed at.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek astocheo (G795), to miss the mark; stochos, a target; mataiologia (G3150), vain talking; anupokritos (G505), unfeigned; agape (G26), charity.

expand to see more

Greek astocheo (G795) — to miss the aim; rendered swerved here and erred twice elsewhere in the Pastorals.

Greek mataiologia (G3150) — empty talking; rendered vain jangling, its only occurrence.

Greek telos (G5056) — the end, the goal aimed at; rendered the end of the commandment.

Greek agape (G26) — love; rendered charity, the mark the commandment aims at.

Greek anupokritos (G505) — without play-acting; rendered faith unfeigned.

Usage

"“some having swerved” — an archer's word, of missing the mark."

"“the end of the commandment is charity” — the mark itself."

"“understanding neither what they say” — confidence outliving comprehension."
